pageNumbering: Physical PDF pages, one-based; page 81 is printed 69
rightsBasis: UCL Press copyright page (physical page 6) and the UCL Discovery record state CC BY 4.0 for this book, including its images. Required attribution: Lily Kahn, The First Hebrew Shakespeare Translations. London, UCL Press, 2017. DOI 10.14324/111.9781911307976.

reviewPoints.acceptance: The title, bilingual-edition subtitle and Lily Kahn byline remain readable; the UCL Press logo remains visible. The present conversion splits the large title into two headings.
Introduction precedes the historical-background section and its opening Haskalah prose. The section line currently becomes a paragraph rather than a nested heading.

reviewPoints.target: Dense parallel English and Hebrew prose
reviewPoints.acceptance: The English left column and Hebrew right column both remain selectable; the Hebrew paragraph has right-to-left direction and its opening phrase appears. The reflow serializes the English column before the Hebrew column and does not retain side-by-side alignment.

reviewPoints.target: Vocalized Hebrew verse, English translation and numbered notes
reviewPoints.acceptance: Both scripts and Hebrew vowel points survive in selectable text; the English opening, a Hebrew vocalized word and numbered note 46 appear in source reading order. Line pairing, exact note attachment and the many Hebrew lines incorrectly promoted to headings remain unqualified.

reviewPoints.target: Bilingual dramatic dialogue with speaker labels and stage directions
reviewPoints.acceptance: The trumpet stage direction and its English dialogue remain text. Speaker, line and parallel-column order are not qualified; the baseline separates some role labels from the lines they introduce.
The Markel, Needler and later Salkinson entries remain selectable in source order; punctuation and typography of individual references remain unqualified.

scope: Physical source pages 5, 13, 81, 150, 250 and 550 were rendered and compared with the no-OCR Hebrew-language EPUB on macOS 27. This is an admission review, not a full-book fidelity claim. The reviewed content contract protects only the explicit phrases and image presence it lists.
